[reverse-keyed]), winning (e.g., "For me, the best feeling in the world comes from winning."), playboy (e.g., "I would find it enjoyable to date more than one person at a time."), violence (e.g., "I think that violence is sometimes necessary."), heterosexual self-presentation (e.g., "I would be furious if someone thought I was gay."), pursuit of status (e.g., "Having status is not important to me."), primacy of work (e.g., "I need to prioritize my work over other things."), power over women (e.g., "I love it when men are in charge of women."), self-reliance (e.g., "I never ask for help."), and risk-taking (e.g., "I put myself in risky situations.") with three items each,1 = strongly disagree,6 = strongly agree.

Both short versions were constructed based on the highest-loading items per subscale in the extensive parent measures (Levant et al., 2013 (Levant et al., , 2020)). We opted for short forms to warrant comparable scale lengths among all utilized masculinity measures while ensuring stable factor structures (Levant et al., 2013 (Levant et al., , 2020) and test economy. The corresponding studies provided satisfactory arguments in favor of construct validity for the short forms of the measures of classical masculinity. Following our endeavor to evaluate the global scores per scale, we computed average scores across all respective items per measure. McDonald's ωs for the utilized short versions of the Male Role Norms Inventory and Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory were .93 and .71, respectively.

Problematic Masculinity

The 15-item Man Box Scale (Hill et al., 2020) and the 28-item Toxic Masculinity Scale (Sanders et al., 2024) purport to supplement classical masculinity concepts. While the Man Box Scale (e.g., "In my opinion, a man should always have the final say about decisions in his relationship or marriage.") does not entail subscales (1 = strongly disagree,2 = disagree,3 = agree,4 = strongly agree), the Toxic Masculinity Scale covers masculine superiority (11 items; e.g., "On average, men are smarter than women."), gender rigidity (nine items; e.g., "Sex workers have no self-respect."), emotional restriction (e.g., "Crying means I am weak."), and repressed suffering (e.g., "If I don't feel well, I just ignore it"; four items each),1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree. We used self-translated versions of both measures, with translation procedures following the same guidelines as the classical masculinity measures. We computed average scores across all items for a measure.

McDonald's ωs for the Man Box Scale and Toxic Masculinity Scale were .94 and .80, respectively.

Stress

To capture stress, we administered the German 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (Schneider et al., 2020). It assesses the frequency with which individuals experience specific thoughts or feelings. Six items tap helplessness (e.g., "In the last month, how often have you felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life?"), four items measure self-efficacy ("In the last month, how often have you felt that you were on top of things?" ; reversed),1 = never,2 = almost never,3 = sometimes,4 = quite often,5 = very often. We used the average score across all items, ω = .68.

Mental Health

To measure the frequency with which participants experience mental health problems (e.g., feeling down, depressed, or hopeless), we used the German nine-item version of the Patient Health Questionnaire (Löwe et al., 2002; original by Spitzer et al., 1999),1 = not at all,2 = on some days,3 = more than half of the day,4 = almost every day, ω = .92.

Aggression

To measure reactive (11 items; e.g., "How often have you reacted angrily when provoked by others") and proactive aggression (12 items; "How often have you used force to obtain money or things from others?"), we used a German adaptation of the Reactive and Proactive Aggression Questionnaire (Raine et al., 2006), as used in Blötner et al. (2025), ωs = .89 and .93, respectively. Rewordings were necessary to match an adult rather than an adolescent sample (as is the case in the original scale),1 = never,2 = sometimes,3 = often.

Motive Dispositions

To measure needs for power (e.g., being in a leadership position in which others work for someone or look to someone for direction), achievement (e.g., importance to take on more difficult and challenging goals and responsibilities), and intimacy (e.g., giving sympathy and love to other people), we administered the respective six-item subscales from the Unified Motives Scale (Schönbrodt & Gerstenberg, 2012). To extend the nomological network, we also included the respective six-item need for affiliation (e.g., trying to be in the company of friends as much as possible) and fear of loss (e.g., being afraid of failing in somewhat difficult situations when a lot depends on oneself) subscales. Some items ask for agreement with statements, others for the importance of goals,1 = strongly disagree/not important to me,2 = disagree/of little importance to me,3 = rather disagree/of some importance to me,4 = rather agree/important to me,5 = agree/very important to me,6 = strongly agree/extremely important to me. Regardless of the response format, items tapping the same subscale were averaged to obtain scores subjected to analyses. McDonald's ωs for fear of loss, need for power, need for affiliation, need for achievement, and need for intimacy were .89, .84, .86, .90, .86, and .86, respectively.

Social Dominance Orientation

To measure a social dominance orientation, we presented a self-translated version of the Social Dominance Orientation 7 (Ho et al., 2015). With eight items each, it assesses dominance (e.g., "No one group should dominate in society."; reverse-keyed) and antiegalitarianism (e.g., "It is unjust to try to make groups equal."),1 = strongly disagree,2 = disagree,3 = neutral,4 = agree,5 = strongly agree. We computed an average score across JINGLE JANGLE IN MASCULINITY RESEARCH 20 items from both subscales, ω = .78.

Right-Wing Authoritarianism

Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with the German Kurzskala Autoritarismus-3 (Short Scale Authoritarianism-3; Beierlein et al., 2015). It measures authoritarian aggression (e.g., "Social rules should be enforced, without mercy."), authoritarian submissiveness (e.g., "We need strong leaders so that we can live safely in society."), and conventionalism (e.g., "Established behaviors should not be questioned.") with three items each,1 = strongly disagree,2 = rather disagree,3 = neutral,4 = rather agree,5 = strongly agree. We computed an average score across items from all subscales, ω = .79.

Openness and Other Broad Personality Features

To measure openness, we used the respective 12-item subscale from the Big Five Inventory-2 (Danner et al., 2019; Soto & John, 2017). To further the nomological network, we also administered the remaining Big Five subscales from the parent measure, each of which temperamental, gets emotional easily"; neuroticism]),1 = strongly disagree,2 = rather disagree,3 = neutral,4 = rather agree,5 = strongly agree. We computed average scores from all items of the same subscale. McDonald's ωs for openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism were .66, .64, .69, .58, and .74, respectively.

Dictator Game

We asked the participants to imagine being allocated a sum of 100€ (approx. $100), which they have to share with another person who cannot intervene. The participants decided on their own how much money they would share, while there would only be one trial and no opportunity for renegotiation. Therein, the gender of the fictitious recipient was manipulated randomly such that the pseudo-receiver was either presented as another man, as a woman, or as a nonbinary person. From the final sample, 348, 349, and 380 participants played the dictator game with a fictitious nonbinary person, with a fictitious man, and with a fictitious woman, respectively. We recorded the sum offered to the virtual respondent as an index of prosociality toward members of different gender groups, with a proposal of 0€ meaning that players would keep the whole sum for themselves (i.e., maximal egotism) and a proposal of 100€ meaning that players would give the whole sum to the receiver (i.e., maximal altruism).

Offers could be made in steps of 1€.

Analysis Plan

Construct Validity

We computed bivariate correlations among all study variables to test the hypotheses H1 to H10. Then, we tested whether masculinity measures and measures of openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism were correlated differently with the other criteria by means of correlation difference tests for dependent correlations as per the Steiger (1980) method. To do so, we used the R package diffcor (version 0.8.4; Blötner, 2024).

To correct for multiple testing, we employed a Type I error rate of α = .001 for all statistical tests. We deviated from our preregistration in the following way: To acknowledge potential commonalities in strengths of associations but different directions considering correlations of masculinity measures vis-à-vis openness with other constructs, we applied correlation difference tests to absolute correlations for these comparisons, that is, to |rs| instead of raw rs.

To evaluate the overall similarity between the correlation profiles of classical and problematic masculinity measures, openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism, we computed the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation (ICCDE) between vectors of correlations, using the R package iccde (version 0.3.8; Blötner & Grosz, 2025).

This metric has been used in previous studies on assumed jingle and jangle fallacies to quantify the similarity between correlation profiles (see Blötner, 2025). Akin to correlations, it can range from -1 to +1, such that the lower threshold is supposed to indicate that constructs reflect mutual opposites and the upper threshold is supposed to indicate that constructs are identical. Within personality research, |ICCDE| ≥ .90 has been frequently interpreted as an indication of (dis)similarity because this level of agreement leaves little space for uniqueness within the correlation profiles subjected to analysis (Blötner, 2025).

Criterion Validity

To test hypotheses H11 and H12, we carried out a hierarchical, moderated regression analysis for each masculinity measure. Therein, the offers made to the recipient in the dictator game served as the criterion, the score of the respective masculinity measures served as the predictor, and the gender of the recipient presented to the participants was the assumed moderator. In case of a significant interaction effect, we computed simple slope analyses. To address potential non-normality of the distribution of the criterion measure, we applied bootstrapping (k = 5,000).

Mutual Incremental Validity of Masculinity Measures Beyond Each Other

In a non-preregistered analysis that can be derived from the framework for tests of jingle and jangle fallacies by Lawson and Robins (2021), we investigated whether the four measures of the endorsement of masculinity norms elicited incremental validity beyond each other in accounting for variance of the aforementioned external constructs. For each pair, we estimated the percentage of variance of the above criteria accounted for by one measure above and beyond the corresponding other measure, employing multiple regression analyses with bootstrapping (k = 5,000, 1-α = .999). Therein, we computed ΔR 2 as the difference between the variance of the corresponding criteria accounted for models with two versus one masculinity measures as predictors and f 2 as the corresponding effect size (Cohen, 1988).

Common Factor Structure

Lawson and Robins' (2021) guidelines for the evaluation of assumed jingle and jangle fallacies propose the evaluation of the uniqueness versus redundancy of two constructs (in our case, traditional and problematic masculinities) by comparing one-factor and two-factor solutions in a confirmatory factor analysis. We added this procedure as a non-preregistered analysis to further obtain evidence for or against our claim of the existence of jingle and jangle fallacies in masculinity research. We used the R package lavaan (version 0.6-21; Rosseel, 2012) to investigate whether a one-factor solution (indicating a jangle fallacy) or a two-factor solution (with distinct but correlated traditional and problematic masculinity factors) would fit better to our data. We did so by specifying two forms of models, namely item-level and parcel-level models, each of which was furthermore tested with hierarchical and non-hierarchical structuring: In the item-level, non-hierarchical variant, we assigned all items directly to the overarching factors (i.e., broad masculinity in the single-factor model; classical and problematic masculinity in the two-factor model). In the item-level hierarchical variants of the single-and two-factor models, we considered the multidimensional structures of all measures by assigning items to their corresponding subscales (as proposed by the original authors), subscales to their corresponding measures, and measures either to (a) an overall factor or (b) to classical or problematic masculinity factors. In the corresponding parcel-level variants, we specified subscale-wise parcels for each measure and assigned these parcels either to scale-level high-order factors (i.e., hierarchical) or directly to broad factors.

We compared fit indices between the corresponding variants and evaluated the latent correlations in the two-factor models.

Emergence of General Masculinity Factors per Measure

In another series of confirmatory factor analyses, we acknowledged recent claims according to which the endorsement of masculinity norms does not reflect a unitary construct (Wong & Wang, 2022) by specifying and testing bifactor structures of the multidimensional measures purported to capture the endorsement of masculinity norms, that is, the Male Role Norms Inventory, the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory, and the Toxic Masculinity Scale. In bifactor models, each item loads onto the specific factor it purports to measure (e.g., a restrictive emotionality factor from the Male Role Norms Inventory) and onto a general factor (e.g., a broad masculinity factor constituted by all items from the Male Role Norms Inventory) that is uncorrelated with all specific factors (see Eid et al., 2018, for an overview).

We inspected the loadings onto the broad factor to examine whether the items in fact constitute a meaningful overall factor. We deemed the assumption of the emergence of a meaningful general factor for a particular measure tenable if its corresponding loadings by and large exceeded λ = .40 (Nunnally & Bernstein, 2017). We conducted these analyses with the R package lavaan (version 0.6-21; Rosseel, 2012).

Exploratory Group Comparisons

As a non-preregistered analysis that was carried out only during the peer-review process, we tested whether participants' sexual orientation was associated with the endorsement of any conceptualization of masculinity. To this end, we carried out Welch tests between the groups of participants who self-identified as heterosexual (n = 955) or nonheterosexual (n = 122). We compared the corresponding average scores of the aforementioned masculinity measures, applying α = .001, and computed Cohen's d as an effect size measure.

The study was preregistered with an analysis plan. The dataset, the preregistration, the analysis script, supplements, and the codebook are publicly available at https://osf.io/z5kmj/overview?view_only=b405004c20df44f288e7032074e195f9. All deviations from the preregistration are reported transparently.

Results

Construct Validity and Similarity Between Correlation Profiles

Table 2 contains the raw correlations of the variables of interest for our research questions among each other and with external constructs. Moreover, the table informs about correlation differences between absolute correlations and overall similarities between correlation profiles as per the ICCDE. As can be seen, and consistent with our hypotheses H1 to H6, classical and problematic masculinities were positively correlated with stress, mental health issues, proactive aggression, reactive aggression, a need for achievement, and a need for power, rs ≥ .12, all ps < .001, unless stated otherwise. Except for the test score of the Male Role Norms Inventory (r = -.09, p = .004), masculinity scores were negatively correlated with a need for intimacy (rs ≤ -.16), which predominantly supports our hypothesis H7. Our hypotheses H8 to H10, in turn, were fully supported because all masculinity scores were positively correlated with a social dominance orientation and right-wing authoritarianism (rs ≥ .46) and negatively with openness, rs ≤ -.21.

Considering the aforementioned correlations pertinent to our hypotheses, many significant correlation differences concerning associations with crucial external constructs occurred (see subscripts in Table 2). Many of these correlation differences did, however, approximate the targeted threshold proposed for our a priori power analyses (Δr ≈ .10), which we considered to be the lower boundary for equivalence (cf. Gignac & Szodorai, 2016). The corresponding correlation differences yielded significance thanks to the comparatively large sample and the strong intercorrelations among masculinity measures,.69 ≤ rs ≤ .83. In line with mostly small differences between correlation coefficients, we found the correlation profiles of masculinity measures to be highly similar, ICCDEs ≥ .95.

The patterns of correlation differences between masculinity measures on the one hand and social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, and openness on the other hand, in turn, were more remarkable, with many Δr > .20. According to Gignac and Szodorai (2016), r = .20 reflects a moderate effect size in personality research. Due to these overall differences, the correlation profiles of masculinity measures exhibited smaller overlaps with those of measures of social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, and openness.

Previous studies treated ICCDEs ≥ .90 as an indicator of redundancy (cf. Blötner, 2025). Thus, our findings suggest that the examined measures of masculinity are distinct from the aforementioned, conceptually broader constructs.

Criterion Validity

Unlike our hypotheses concerning construct validity, our hypotheses concerning criterion validity were not supported. Contrary to our H11, neither masculinity measure was significantly correlated with offers in the dictator game. This observation held both in correlation analyses in which the recipient's gender was not considered (Table 2) and in regression analyses that controlled for the recipient's gender (Table 3).

Our H12 proposed an interaction between masculinity and the gender of the recipient in the prediction of the offer made to this recipient in the dictator game. Specifically, we expected individuals high in any masculinity concept to make smaller offers to women and nonbinary individuals than to another man. As can be seen in Table 3, however, neither main effects nor interaction effects occurred for any masculinity score. Furthermore, main effects occurred for the recipient's gender, such that women were offered higher sums than men. The respective differences in the offers made to male and nonbinary recipients were nonsignificant (see also our Open Science Framework supplement under https://osf.io/z5kmj/files/osfstorage?view_only=b405004c20df44f288e7032074e195f9 for information about offers made contingent on the recipient's gender). Altogether, these findings do not support our H12.

Mutual Incremental Validity

Table S1 in the Open Science Framework supplement presents the findings from the analyses of mutual incremental validity for the outlined external characteristics. As can be seen, in most cases, masculinity measures did not elicit substantial percentages of incremental validity beyond each other when it comes to accounting for variance of the external criteria, most ps > .001. In many cases in which the percentage of incremental validity was significant, the differences were very small, ΔR2 ≤ .02, f2 ≤ .02 (Cohen, 1988). Of note, however, several percentages of incremental validity achieved moderate levels according to the convention by Cohen (1988; i.e., ΔR2 ≈ .13, f2 ≈ .15), but these cases seldom appeared.

Common Factor Structure

Due to convergence issues, only one of the eight abovementioned confirmatory factor analyses could be fit to the present data, namely the item-level, non-hierarchical single-factor model. The corresponding fit measures indicated less than acceptable fit, χ 2 (4277) = 38,402.61, p < .001, CFI = .75, RMSEA = .09, SRMR = .09 (see Table S2 in our Open Science Framework supplement). Due to the convergence issues of the remaining, alternative models, we were unable to evaluate the common structure of classical and problematic masculinity measures. Problems during the model estimation can likely be attributed to

Emergence of General Masculinity Factors per Measure

Our Open Science Framework supplement entails all information about the conducted bifactor analyses. These analyses revealed that the bifactor model of the utilized version of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory did not converge. From 30 item loadings onto the general factor, 10 fell short of λ = .40. In contrast, the bifactor models for the utilized version of the Male Role Norms Inventory and for the Toxic Masculinity Scale yielded mostly acceptable fit, χ 2 (168-322) = 1,500.37-2,035.92, ps < .001, CFI = .96-.97, RMSEA = .07-.09, SRMR = .04-.05. Akin to the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory, five of the 24 items of the Toxic Masculinity Scale exhibited loadings λ < .40 onto the corresponding bifactor, suggesting that no comprehensive general factor can be assumed for these measures.

In turn, all item loadings from the utilized 21-item version of the Male Role Norms Inventory exceeded λ = .40, indicating the emergence of a meaningful general factor for this measure.

Exploratory Group Comparisons

Men who self-identified as heterosexual scored higher on all masculinity measures than men who self-identified as non-heterosexual, all ps < .001, all Cohen's ds ≥ .37. Table 4 contains the corresponding descriptive statistics and test information.

Discussion

To improve conceptual clarity in masculinity research, this research set out to examine jingle and jangle issues in the research area of the endorsement of masculinity norms. First, heterogeneous conceptualizations of the endorsement of masculinity implied that existing measures for this phenomenon tapped into disparate constructs (Smiler, 2004; Thompson & Bennett, 2015; Thompson et al., 1992; see also Table 1). Second, harmful masculinity (Hill et al., 2020) and toxic masculinity (Horton et al., 2026; Sanders et al., 2024) as allegedly new constructs purport to augment the scope of traditional conceptualizations, but their authors did not provide empirical evidence about the novelty or uniqueness of what we collectively referred to as problematic masculinities. Third, regardless of the label used, empirical endeavors to justify the uniqueness of the masculinity construct in light of the existence of established yet conceptually broader constructs such as openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism were quite simplistic and rested on exaggeratedly strict tenets.

To address these aspects through a more differentiated statistical approach, compared to those employed by earlier researchers who raised the same research question (e.g., Parent et al., 2011), we compared the nomological networks of the overall aggregate scores of eligible measures of the construct(s) under scrutiny. The data was collected in a large sample of German men. Because the correlation profiles of the overall scores of masculinity measures were highly similar, our findings cast substantial doubts about the novelty of toxic and harmful masculinities beyond aggregates of classical conceptualizations of masculinity. In turn, suspected jingle issues among overall scores of traditional masculinity measures and suspected jangle issues with respect to overlaps with openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism could not be supported.

Construct Validity

We argued initially that decisions made in the process of test development would have accounted for the multitude of structures of masculinity within different measures (see Table 1). Accordingly, we suspected the emergence of bloated specifics, that is, pseudo-facets of masculinity that occurred due to the over-representation of particular item contents (Cattell & Tsujioka, 1964). We expected this structural heterogeneity to account for, at best, modest intercorrelations among composite scores of masculinity measures. Contrary to this notion, composites of masculinity measures elicited very high intercorrelations and a high agreement between the correlation profiles with external variables (see Table 2), suggesting that the overall scores actually tap into the same construct. At first glance, however, the host of correlation differences with external constructs stands out. That said, closer inspection reveals that many correlation difference tests were significant even in the case of comparatively small numerical differences. This can be explained by high intercorrelations between the compared scores and the relatively large sample size, both of which mostly exceeded our assumptions for the a priori power analysis: More specifically, over-sampling (ntarget = 1,020; nempirical = 1,077) and slightly stronger than expected intercorrelations among masculinity measures occurred (rtarget = .70; rempirical, median = .76). Both aspects increased the statistical power to detect differences we deemed negligible (Δr ≤ .10; cf. Gignac & Szodorai, 2016). For instance, the composite scores of the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Conformity to Masculinity Norms Inventory were correlated with the compassion facet of agreeableness at rs = -.43 and -.35, respectively, and this difference was significant at p < .001 because the two masculinity measures were correlated at r = .69.

Our pre-registered analyses revealed a clear pattern of the relationship between overall scores of traditional and problematic masculinities. In addition, we sought to add to our argument by running non-preregistered tests of mutual incremental validity, which further informed our analyses of jingle and jangle fallacies. Most cases in which at least moderate levels of mutual incremental validity occurred regarded characteristics with high centrality for the understanding of the effects of the endorsement of masculinity, such as traditional views on society (reflected through right-wing authoritarianism), a social dominance orientation, a need for power, mental health, and proactive aggression (Di Bianca & Mahalik, 2022; Mahalik et al., 2003).

Altogether, strong intercorrelations, numerous negligible correlation differences with external constructs, the extremely high similarity between the total correlation profiles, and mostly negligible levels of mutual incremental validity in predictions of external variables render our initial suspicion about a jingle fallacy for overall scores of classical masculinity measures untenable. Instead, the composite scores of two tested measures for the assessment of the endorsement of masculinity norms mostly tap the same underlying phenomena, regardless of the underlying structure, because virtually the same conclusions concerning our hypotheses held for the overall scores of the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Conformity to Masculinity Norms Inventory. More specifically, and consistent with the notion of a tough self-display and the denial of negative sensations (Addis & Mahalik, 2003; Mahalik et al., 2007; Parent et al., 2011), the overall scores of the endorsement of masculinity norms as per the aforementioned measures went along with higher stress experience and poorer mental health. At the same time, and consistent with earlier studies, composite scores of the endorsement of masculinity as per these concepts were associated with more frequent use of proactive and reactive aggression (e.g., Harrington et al., 2021; Horton et al., 2026), striving for performance and power (Mahalik et al., 2003; Walker et al., 2000), beliefs in the justification of differences between social groups (such as women and sexual minorities), and conservative views about society (Hill et al., 2020; Heilman et al., 2017; Horton et al., 2026; Mahalik et al., 2003; Sanders et al., 2024).

Some findings regarding the overall score of the Male Role Norms Inventory, however, require differentiation. For instance, although the Male Role Norms Inventory includes item content aimed at low display of emotionality (facet entitled restrictive emotionality; see Table 1), endorsement of masculinity norms as per the composite of the Male Role Norms Inventory was less strongly correlated than other masculinity measures with scores of neuroticism and stress symptoms. Additionally, the Male Role Norms Inventory includes a facet dealing with toughness (reflecting risk-taking and being brave and ready for fights; Levant et al., 2013), but its total score yielded the weakest correlations of all masculinity measures with aggression constructs. Last, our H7 positing the endorsement of masculinity to be negatively associated with a need for intimacy could be supported for composite scores of all masculinity measures except that of the Male Role Norms Inventory.

In this regard, it must be noted that the aforementioned measures differ with respect to the assumed origins of the perceived pressure to comply with masculinity norms. More specifically, the items from the Male Role Norms Inventory emphasize perceived external drivers (i.e., other-ascribed masculinity), whereas the items of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory pinpoint an individual's own desire to adhere to masculine standards (Levant et al., 1992; Mahalik et al., 2003). Considering the wordings from the two measures of problematic masculinity, it stands to reason that the corresponding "standards" also reflect fundamental beliefs of an individual rather than norms that were predominantly imposed on this individual. Differences in the suggested extrinsic (versus intrinsic) origins of the norms or standards captured in the measures likely accounted for the smaller effect sizes observed for the Male Role Norms Inventory.

At the same time, our analyses suggest that the two measures purported to measure what we refer to as problematic masculinity (Toxic Masculinity Scale and Man Box Scale) add little beyond classical masculinity: Beyond the uncertainties related to the conceptual novelty derived from the underlying definitions (see above), their composite scores exhibited extremely strong correlations with the composite scores of classical masculinity measures, elicited predominantly negligible correlation differences vis-à-vis external constructs, their overall correlation profiles virtually mirrored those of classical masculinity measures, and they yielded substantial incremental validity only in a few cases (see Tables 2 and 3). Of note, the constructs assembling the domains in which problematic masculinities purport to augment classical masculinity (i.e., stress, mental health, and neuroticism [Hill et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2024]) were similarly correlated with overall scores of problematic and classical conceptualizations of masculinity-casting doubts about whether problematic masculinities actually afford the intended purpose. Such conceptual and psychometric redundancy fragments the literature and stalls meaningful theoretical progress. Addressing this jangle fallacy is therefore essential to equip researchers and practitioners with the precise tools needed to further our understanding of modern masculinities and the societal as well as mental health implications concomitant with the endorsement of strict masculinity norms (e.g., Haslop et al., 2024; Love et al., 2025).

Last, our findings did not suggest that overall scores of any conceptualization of masculinity were reducible to low openness to experience, a social dominance orientation, or right-wing authoritarianism. Despite certain conceptual overlaps, the endorsement of masculinity norms reflects domain-specific prescriptive norms about motives, goals, and behaviors allegedly deemed prototypically male (e.g., status, power, heteronormativity).

These aspects intersect with-but cannot be collapsed to-the generalized values and ideologies concomitant with social dominance orientation or right-wing authoritarianism (Beierlein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2015). Similarly, the defining aspects of the endorsement of masculinity norms cannot be reduced to dispositional openness, as the latter also comprises enjoyment of culture and unconventional ideas about seeing the world (Costa & McCrae, 1992).

Criterion Validity

Of note, our hypotheses that build on offers made in the dictator game could not be supported. That is, neither was any masculinity measure significantly correlated with overall offers made, nor was this relation moderated by the gender of the recipient. We argue in this regard that the imaginary setting of the dictator game did not afford the desired demand characteristics an incentivized dictator game would have engendered, limiting ecological validity. Given the absence of advantages related to egotism, most participants did not make unfair offers (see the distribution of offers in our Open Science Framework supplement). This pattern is consistent with the study by Zhao et al. (2017) in which participants kept more money to themselves if they played for real money rather than being asked to only imagine the redistribution scenario. Thus, incentivization may have altered the patterns of offers made. Interestingly, in this regard, offers made to an imaginary female interaction partner were significantly higher than offers made to imaginary male (d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.23, 0.44]) or nonbinary interaction partners, d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.20, 0.42] (see our supplement). We suspect that the manipulation of recipients' gender reflected a demand characteristic towards gentlemanly behavior. More specifically, participants may have perceived social role expectations that request men to showcase benevolence towards women (Gough & Novikova, 2020), and thus, social desirability may have been at play (Komlenac et al., 2023).

Alternatively, participants could have resorted to benevolent sexism. These considerations are highly speculative, however, given the low overall variance in observed offers in our dictator game. Furthermore, no single item in our item pool could be used as a proxy for the endorsement of "gentleman norms" or benevolent sexism, which could have served as a moderator in the relationship between the endorsement of masculinity norms at large and offers made to recipients with different genders. Future research might, therefore, test whether such tendencies moderate the relationship between the endorsement of masculinity norms and prosociality towards women.

Structural Considerations

Note that in the aforementioned sections, we highlighted that all conclusions drawn from our data refer to overall or composite scores of the endorsement of any masculinity concept. We applied our analyses to overall scores to ensure that the corresponding contents assigned to the same broad umbrella term-masculinity-are comparable across conceptualizations. This being said, the respective facets proposed in the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory and the Male Role Norms Inventory usually do not constitute comprehensive overall masculinity factors as many facets frequently yield only small or even negative correlations among each other (Levant et al., 1992; Mahalik et al., 2003; Wong & Wang, 2022). Bifactor analyses of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory and the Toxic Masculinity Scale indicated that no comprehensive general factors-besides the corresponding specific factors-can be assumed for these measures. In contrast, the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Man Box Scale constitute meaningful overall factors, as suggested through good model fit for single-or bifactor models along with high loadings onto the corresponding general factors (see our Open Science Framework supplement). As such, the emergence of a general factor reflecting the endorsement of masculinity norms depends on the utilized measure. This notion opposes previous claims according to which it would be misleading to compute overall scores of masculinity measures because they would not constitute such general factors (Wong & Wang, 2022). Another caveat regards convergence issues in the preregistered analyses of the common factor structure of classical and problematic masculinities. By means of common confirmatory factor analyses, we sought to establish whether classical and problematic masculinities are better understood as two (at best moderately) correlated factors or as one comprehensive factor. Our non-preregistered standalone confirmatory factor analyses of each measure were already confronted with specific challenges, such as failure to establish general factors for some of the masculinity measures. These issues related to each measure per se further exacerbate the emergence of comprehensive problematic versus classical masculinity factors or even a comprehensive general masculinity factor. We would like to note, however, that (a) the manifest overall test scores of the masculinity measures exhibited very high correlations among each other (rs ≈ .70 and above), (b) virtually identical nomological networks occurred for the overall scores of the four measures, and (c) the overall scores of the measures yielded only limited mutual incremental validity beyond each other. Notably, the inability to successfully estimate the proposed latent structure does not invalidate the remaining analyses. Therefore, we argue that claims about the same construct being measured by the overall scores of the four masculinity measures can also be made without confirmatory factor analyses emphasizing the superiority of a single-factor model or findings of two extremely highly correlated latent factors (cf. Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

Limitations, Future Directions, Constraints on Generality, and Practical Implications

This research was affected by some limitations. First, our sample was quite heterogeneous with respect to age and education, but less so with respect to sexual orientation. Although the endorsement of masculinity norms regards individuals irrespective of their sexual orientations (Komlenac et al., 2023; Thompson & Bennett, 2015), nonheterosexual individuals should differ considerably from heterosexual individuals in their responses to items about the enforcement of heteronormativity-a theme captured in all masculinity measures employed in the present research. More specifically, "heterosexual men may consider masculine norms to be aligned with an identity they view as proximal, while sexual minority men may view traditional masculinity as inapplicable to their sense of self" (Anghel et al., 2023 (Anghel et al., , p. 2321)). That said, the 30 item-version of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory yields scalar measurement invariance across sexual orientation (Anghel et al., 2023; Komlenac et al., 2023), lending support to the notion that the same construct is being assessed across sexual orientations. The same does not hold, however, for the Male Role Norms Inventory, in which heteronormativity is more centrally represented than in the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (McDermott et al., 2021). The two measures of problematic masculinity entail an even larger ratio of items tapping heteronormative ideation, suggesting that they are ineligible for use in samples of individuals with a sexual orientation other than heterosexual. Establishing measurement non-invariance for these measures would lend further support to the abovementioned notion concerning the limited usefulness of the Toxic Masculinity Scale and the Man Box Scale. This being said, our exploratory findings according to which heterosexual men scored higher on global scores of all masculinity measures than non-heterosexual mean should be interpreted with caution, especially in the case of the measures for which measurement invariance could not (yet) be established (but see also our considerations above about the raison d'être of a general factor within the aforementioned masculinity measures).

Another aspect regarding the sample refers to its restriction to German men. That said, the cultural background within which an individual is socialized determines the norms to which this individual is expected to comply (Thompson & Bennett, 2015). For instance, attitudes towards gender roles differ in their scope and dimensionality across different cultures (Constantin & Voicu, 2015). In line with this, several participants indicated at the end of our survey that they did not understand specific contents or that specific aspects did not apply to them. For instance, the use of personal pronouns was covered by specific items of the utilized masculinity measures, while the explicit sharing of the preferred personal pronouns (e.g., he/him) is less common in Germany than in the US context, in which all the measures administered in our study were developed originally. More specifically, the classical masculinity measures administered in our study were developed by collecting masculinity standards as endorsed in American culture (e.g., Levant et al., 1992; Mahalik et al., 2003). As such, it stands to reason that the covered standards of masculinity are entangled with specifics of American culture, but these American masculinity standards do not necessarily generalize to other cultures (see Thompson & Bennett, 2015, for an overview of diverse, culture-specific masculinity concepts and operationalizations). This culture-blindness is also reflected in a lack of cultural attunement in masculinity measures beyond those investigated here (Fisher et al., 2026). For example, the levels of acceptability of the use of aggression and the search for as well as the display of status differ across cultures (Hofstede et al., 2010). Since cultural differences determine the masculinity norms a person endorses, more research is needed about cross-cultural measurement invariance of the assessment tools applied therein. Another ambitious endeavor in this regard would comprise the distillation of masculinity norms that hold across cultures.

Third, our study rested primarily on self-reports, with numerous sources of response distortion being well-documented (Podsakoff et al., 2012). We aimed to supplement the set of self-report measures with a measure reflecting a behavioral proxy, namely the dictator game.

A broad set of constructs is advantageous to provide nuanced and well-founded conclusions about the redundancy versus uniqueness of psychological constructs in the sense of examinations of jingle and jangle fallacies (Blötner, 2025). Thus, in future research, a larger set of behavioral measures (or proxies thereof) should be applied to discern the endorsement of masculinity norms from one another or from other closely related constructs.

Last, our study purposefully addressed the redundancy of the administered masculinity measures at the composite score level to capture the entirety of masculinity standards of each conceptualization. Using even larger and more diverse samples, future work would arguably benefit from employing latent variable approaches that more directly evaluate the extent to which all available measures reflect common versus unique variance (e.g., bifactor or related structural models). Such approaches may provide a more direct test of whether these instruments primarily reflect a common masculinity factor or whether meaningful specific dimensions remain after accounting for shared variance.

Conclusion

Our findings provide clear evidence that overall scores of toxic and harmful masculinity do not constitute constructs that can be distinguished from overall scores computed for classical masculinities. Instead, composites of toxic and harmful masculinity concepts align almost perfectly with composites of classical masculinity measures, indicating a jangle fallacy at least at the level of the global measures. In contrast, suspected jingle issues among composites of classical masculinity measures were not supported. Despite structural differences, total scores of classical measures exhibited very high intercorrelations and nearly identical patterns of associations with external constructs. These results indicate that global scores of classical masculinity tap the same underlying construct. Simultaneously, they offer theoretical value beyond broader traits such as openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism, from which they were clearly distinguishable. The non-incentivized and imaginary nature of the applied variant of the dictator game likely limited behavioral differentiations, suggesting that future work should incorporate incentivized or other ecologically valid behavioral measures.

What has not yet been evaluated in detail regards the existence of redundancies versus distinctions at the level of the facets of classical, harmful, and toxic masculinities. The search for a comprehensive structure from all available contents was beyond the scope of this research, but it remains a promising outlook for future studies. In this regard, we encourage consolidation rather than further expansion of masculinity constructs, alongside future work that incorporates behavioral indicators. Likewise, cultural and measurement-invariance issues should be addressed to strengthen construct validity in masculinity research.
